paragraphs: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers do not only handle placement or only handle the brand: this occupational category covers both roles delivered as advertising and promotional campaigns (O*NET 11-2011.00) and marketing management roles delivered as marketing strategy, pricing, and product mix (O*NET 11-2021.00). The two share audience and competitor analysis, budgets, and metrics, but their deliverables and scope of responsibility differ; this page explains employment and wages on the BLS combined-entry basis and, where needed, labels the figures for each occupation separately.

Start with a small exercise that can be completed within three days: choose a fictional category, write the target customer and competitor judgment, three verifiable claims, one pricing or channel assumption, a budget allocation, and metrics, then write a one-page review explaining how you would adjust. Record the time you spent checking demand and competitor material, how many times you revised your assumptions, and whether you are willing to write creative judgment and budget trade-offs into handover-ready material. This is only an entry-level slice and cannot represent marketing management competence.

Observable signals that someone may fit better include: being able to explain the basis for a judgment from customer demand, the competitive landscape, and financial constraints at the same time; being willing to revise your own judgment with data; habitually writing assumptions, definitions, and limits into reviewable records; and being able to drive a decision to delivery amid cross-team disagreement. Be cautious if you would rather only execute creative work, dislike dealing with budgets and people issues, or lack patience for metric definitions and competitor information; marketing management roles usually also require several years of relevant experience first.
This is exploratory advice; it must be checked together with your interests, hands-on task experience, and the job conditions of the target market, and cannot replace your own judgment.

The core exchange of this work is turning market and customer information into an executable marketing plan: judging demand and competition, setting the positioning and pricing direction, organizing advertising and promotional campaigns, allocating the budget, and reviewing with metrics. Judging fit should depend on whether you are willing to trade off repeatedly among data, creative, and organizational collaboration, and to accept the reality that management roles usually require relevant work experience first; interest and personality assessments serve only as clues.

BLS combines advertising, promotions, and marketing managers into one entry: plan programmes to generate interest in a product or service. Within it, O*NET 11-2011.00 advertising and promotions managers plan, direct, or coordinate advertising policies and programmes and produce promotional material; O*NET 11-2021.00 marketing managers plan marketing policies and programmes, identify potential customers, set pricing strategy, and monitor demand for new products.

entries: Advertising and promotions | Define the audience and claims | Research consumer opinions and buying habits, identify the target audience, and write the creative brief and verifiable claims.
Advertising and promotions | Organize material and media | Check layouts and copy, edit scripts and material, coordinate placement arrangements with media, and prepare budgets and cost estimates.

Marketing management | Demand and competitor judgment | Analyse business development and market trends, determine demand for products and services, and identify potential customers and competitor movements.

Section heading | Work environment and methods for advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
Direct answer | This occupational category contains two kinds of role: advertising and promotions managers, delivered as advertising and promotional campaigns, and marketing managers, delivered as marketing strategy, pricing, and product mix; both work in office settings, communicate frequently with internal teams and external partners, and travel arranged around clients or media.
Common organizations and locations | Marketing managers are employed mainly in professional, scientific, and technical services and in corporate and enterprise management; advertising and promotions managers are employed mainly in professional, scientific, and technical services and the information sector.
Work materials and systems | Common materials include market and competitor analysis, creative briefs, creative material and scripts, media and budget plans, pricing and product proposals, campaign boards, and performance reviews; common tools include analytics, customer relationship management, design, and office software.
How tasks are organized | Work proceeds through demand and competitor judgment, strategy and budget, material and channels, execution, and review: first set the target customer and the basis for judgment, then form the strategy and budget plan, complete approvals and execute, and evaluate against metrics whether to adjust.
Deadlines and work intensity | Intensity concentrates on plan reviews, campaign launches, and quarterly reviews: O*NET work context shows that among marketing managers 84% of respondents work more than 40 hours a week, 90% use the telephone every day for communication, and 78% sit almost continuously.
Collaboration and reporting lines | Work is usually done with sales, product, design, media, finance, and research teams, reporting to a business lead or the client side; product licensing, legal opinion, and platform review rest with the responsible authorized parties.
Review and accountability chain | A plan must pass budget approval, brand and compliance checks, and approval by the business authorizer; pricing and contracts follow organizational authority and are documented.
Quality and professional requirements | Quality depends on whether the demand judgment is evidence-based, whether positioning and pricing have a basis, whether the budget has boundaries, and whether the performance metrics match the goals.

'Technical tractability' answers only whether a tool is capable of completing a class of tasks; it does not mean an organization has adopted it, nor that jobs have therefore declined. Judging this layer means looking at whether a tool can reliably produce usable results: for example, organizing publicly available competitor information or generating copy variants, where it can produce a first draft, but demand judgment, positioning trade-offs, and pricing decisions still require a person to be accountable.

'Actual organizational adoption' asks whether organizations really put the tool into their processes. For marketing and advertising work, adoption thresholds include customer data authorization, material copyright, brand and platform rules, the approval chain, and whether the team can measure error cost (such as the cost of mispricing or an improper commitment). Technical availability does not mean it will be adopted.

'Job numbers and work redistribution' is another layer of the question: even if tasks are partly automated, job numbers may rise or fall with market demand and budget changes.
